summary: Describes a framework for using forward error correction codes with applications in IP networks to protect against packet loss. It supports applying FEC to arbitrary packet flows over unreliable transport, mainly for real-time or streaming media.

plainLanguage.summary: The FEC Framework lets packet-delivery protocols use separately specified methods to recover lost data. It defines shared packet and configuration rules but leaves each error-correction method to its own specification.

questions: how does fec recover lost packets
subtitle: A framework for protecting packet flows with compatible forward error correction schemes.

tldr.problem: Streaming packet flows may lose data, and each delivery protocol would otherwise need to define how its own forward error correction works.
tldr.mechanism: The framework groups application data units into source blocks and gives them to a separate FEC scheme. The scheme returns repair packets that the receiver can use to recover missing source data.
tldr.outcome: Content delivery protocols and FEC schemes can be specified independently. Repair traffic must not exceed source traffic and must adapt when congestion control changes the source rate.

today: RFC 6363 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2011. It has been updated by RFC 8680; RFC 6364 defines related SDP elements.

sections.title: What Forward Error Correction Covers
sections.content:
Many applications send packet streams over networks that do not guarantee delivery. Forward Error Correction (FEC) adds encoded data so a receiver may reconstruct lost packets without asking for retransmission. RFC 6363 focuses on detectable loss, called erasure, rather than packets received in corrupted form.

The framework is intended for arbitrary packet flows over unreliable transports such as UDP, especially real-time or streaming media. It defines the parts common to FEC-based Content Delivery Protocols (CDPs), not a complete CDP. It does not specify how a sender chooses flows or signals their configuration to a receiver.
sections.plainLanguage: FEC adds data that can help recover packets that never arrived. This RFC defines shared rules for adding that protection to packet flows.

sections.title: The Framework and the FEC Scheme
sections.content:
The FEC Framework sits between a transport layer, such as UDP or DCCP, and protocols above it. It handles application data units (ADUs) belonging to packet flows. A FEC scheme performs the actual encoding and decoding and defines the identifiers used to interpret source and repair packets.

At the sender, the framework passes ADUs to the scheme and receives repair symbols and payload IDs. At the receiver, it passes source and repair payloads to the scheme and receives recovered source payloads. RTP may carry source packets, repair packets, both or neither, according to the chosen scheme.
sections.plainLanguage: The framework organizes the data and passes it to a separate FEC scheme. The scheme creates repair data and attempts to reconstruct missing data at the receiver.

sections.title: Sender and Receiver Steps
sections.content:
The sender groups an ordered sequence of ADUs into a source block and gives the block to the FEC scheme. The scheme returns repair payloads and their Repair FEC Payload IDs, and may return Source FEC Payload IDs. The framework builds source and repair packets and sends them using normal transport procedures.

The receiver removes an explicit source ID when present and passes packet data and IDs to the scheme. The scheme groups packets into blocks. If a block has missing source packets and enough repair data arrives, it can reconstruct some or all of the missing payloads. Recovery is not guaranteed, and packets may reach the application out of order.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender groups data and sends both original and repair packets. The receiver uses the repair packets to try to fill gaps in each group.

sections.title: Source Packets, Repair Packets and Configuration
sections.content:
A source packet contains the original ADU and may have an Explicit Source FEC Payload ID appended. If the scheme can derive the identifier from another field, no extra field is needed. A repair packet contains a Repair FEC Payload ID followed by repair symbols; when carried over RTP, it also has an RTP header.

The framework configuration identifies protected source flows, repair flows, the FEC Encoding ID, the source-ID length and any FEC-scheme-specific information. A CDP specification must define how the sender and receiver obtain this information. One recommended generic source identifier is a two-octet unsigned sequence number.
sections.plainLanguage: Source packets carry original data and may carry an extra identifier. Repair packets carry a repair identifier and the encoded data needed by the selected scheme.

sections.title: What a FEC Scheme Must Specify
sections.content:
A FEC scheme used with this framework must process source blocks of ADUs. Its specification must give a unique IANA-registered FEC Encoding ID, the format of its Repair FEC Payload ID, and the names and encoding rules for scheme-specific information.

The specification must define the FEC code precisely enough to determine the symbols in each repair packet. It must also describe practical encoding and decoding algorithms. A scheme may define an Explicit Source FEC Payload ID, and its encoded fields must have fixed or derivable lengths.
sections.plainLanguage: A scheme's specification must explain its identifiers, data formats and encoding code. It must also show that senders and receivers can carry out the encoding and decoding.

sections.title: Feedback, Congestion and Security
sections.content:
Applications using feedback for congestion control MUST calculate it from packets received before FEC recovery. Otherwise recovered data could hide packet loss and give congestion control a misleading view of the network. The framework is not intended to overcome loss caused by heavy congestion.

FEC repair bandwidth MUST NOT exceed source bandwidth, and repair rate MUST change when congestion control changes the source rate. FEC itself provides no confidentiality or integrity. The RFC recommends protecting both source and repair packets and protecting configuration and payload IDs from alteration.
sections.plainLanguage: Congestion control must measure what arrived before repair, so lost packets remain visible. Repair traffic must stay within the source rate, and separate security measures must protect the data.
